articles.title: How Burnham’s 10-year plan can turn more happiness into higher growth
articles.summary: Solely targeting GDP is the road to ruin. A wider focus is needed, from better youth and mental health services to more apprenticeships. When Andy Burnham publishes his 10-year plan, he is expected to define what the UK government can do to help and support citizens of all ages.
body: In a story arc refreshing the idea of a modern, “cradle to grave” welfare state, the document will, according to some sources, define what the state can do for young people, those in middle age, and older people.

There is furious lobbying going on right now to determine what goes in the document, which is understandable when the measures that are included will form the basis of policy for at least the next few years, even if the plan itself fails to last intact for a decade. Burnham has pledged to publish it by mid-December.

The public is almost certainly going to read comforting words about the need to lift more children out of poverty and support them into well-paid jobs. That is Alan Milburn’s victory after his landmark report earlier this month.
However, people need Burnham to say more about how he intends to approach this subject; will he revert to language that emphasises how individual measures increase economic growth?

articles.title: Sisters strike back: have women finally had enough of the caring burden?
articles.summary: When elderly parents need looking after, it’s usually their daughters who do the bulk of the work – as highlighted by a viral Saturday Night Live skit. Here, siblings share how to spread the load more evenly. When Simran and her older brother were growing up, he was always the golden boy.
body: “It’s funny how the tables have turned,” she says. “The person they spoiled is the person who has never been there for them, never even bought my mum and dad a birthday card. I had dreams and ambitions of things I wanted to do, but I can’t pursue them now.”

As a woman of south Asian heritage, Simran says she is also battling an extra cultural expectation that she will look after her parents. “I had a friend say: ‘But you are really blessed to have to do seva,’” she says, referring to the Sikh tradition of selfless service for others. “And I say: ‘Blessed in what way?’ Of course I want to be there for my mum … but people don’t get it unless they’re a carer, how lonely and isolating it is, how it affects your mental health.”

articles.title: Chocolate Mousse With Salty Orange Whip
articles.summary: Chocolate mousse is always a good idea—a classic for a reason. The bitterness of chocolate is paired with a lightly sweet and salty cream, but it tastes just as good on its own.
body: To make the chocolate mousse: In a medium saucepan over medium heat, heat 113 g (½ cup) heavy cream until steaming. Remove from the heat and add 170 g (scant 1 cup) coarsely chopped 60% to 70% dark chocolate. Whisk until smooth. Transfer to a medium bowl and let cool to room temperature, about 20 minutes.

Meanwhile, in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment (or in a large bowl with a whisk or handheld mixer), whisk together the remaining 227 g (about 1 cup) heavy cream, 1½ Tbsp. powdered sugar, and ¼ tsp. kosher salt until stiff peaks form, about 4 minutes. Using a rubber spatula, fold a small amount of the whipped cream into the chocolate mixture until combined, then gently fold in the remaining cream, making sure to not beat in too much air. Spoon the mousse into eight serving bowls, cover, and refrigerate for at least 2 hours or up to 4 days.
points: Chocolate mousse is always a good idea—a classic for a reason.
The bitterness of chocolate is paired with a lightly sweet and salty cream, but it tastes just as good on its own.

articles.title: A Flavor-Filled Trip Around Veracruz with Chef Lucho Martínez
articles.summary: The Mexico City-based chef, who's restaurant Em was one of the first in the capital to be awarded a Michelin star, shows us around his home state, sharing the places and ingredients that continue to inspire him.
body: It was a Sunday morning at the El Tajín archaeological site in the state of Veracruz, and the entrance was humming with people selling embroidered dresses and glazed ceramics. Once we were past the gate, however, the crowds thinned, and we could marvel at the pre-Columbian pyramids in quietude. “When I come during the week, it's completely empty,” said Lucho Martínez, chef and founder of Mexico City's Michelin-starred restaurant Em, as we circled the main building. Believed to have been built by the Totonac people, it's a magnificent six-terraced structure with 365 carved niches set against the backdrop of lush hills. “It feels forgotten,” he said, glancing around the stillness.

Martínez, who remains one of Mexico City's most exciting chefs, hopes to use his platform to spotlight the region where he was born, emphasizing its exceptional produce. He also wants to change its perception and prove it's more than ports and oil refineries. “Nobody talks about its vanilla or coffee or all the produce it has,” said Martínez, who sources 90 percent of his ingredients from Veracruz, including vanilla, for Em.

articles.title: Sacha Beef
articles.summary: For anyone who grew up in Taiwan, sacha is a very nostalgic flavor. It's extremely savory and just barely sweet, and is a go-to flavor for stir-fries at Taiwanese beer houses.
body: Marinate the beef: Take 12 oz. (340 g) beef chuck and look for large pieces of muscle, pulling them apart with your hands and slicing away connective tissue to separate each piece. (While you’re at it, trim away any silver skin you see, as it tends to be chewy.) Cut these muscle-y chunks against the grain and into thin slices about 1" by ½" (2.5 by 1.3 cm).

In a large bowl, combine the beef slices, 1 egg white, whisked until slightly foamy, 1½ tsp. sugar, ¾ tsp. cornstarch, ½ tsp. baking soda, ½ tsp. kosher salt, 2 Tbsp. unsalted Shaoxing rice wine, such as huadiao, or sherry in a pinch, 1 Tbsp. sacha sauce, and 1½ tsp. water. Mix well and store in the fridge for at least 2 hours and up to overnight (12 hours max).
Now to assemble: Chop 1 large head A-choy (3½ oz. / 100 g) into thirds, roughly 2" (5 cm) long and set aside. Remove the marinated beef from the fridge.

Heat a wok or heavy-bottomed pan over high heat and drizzle in 1 Tbsp. neutral oil, such as canola. Once the oil is hot and looks loose, slide in the beef. Sauté, stirring every so often, until mostly cooked through and browned all over, about 3 minutes. Remove the beef and set aside.
points: For anyone who grew up in Taiwan, sacha is a very nostalgic flavor.
It's extremely savory and just barely sweet, and is a go-to flavor for stir-fries at Taiwanese beer houses.

articles.title: Inside the Making of Dolly Alderton’s Lavish New ‘Pride and Prejudice’
articles.summary: As a generation awaits its own adaptation of “Pride and Prejudice,” screenwriter Dolly Alderton shares her funny, intimate, and illuminating day-to-day diary of making the television event of the year.
body: As I leave, she gives me a big hug. “Mate, it’s gonna be brilliant.” True sisterhood.
The day I have been dreading. Cuts. Lisa (producer) reassured me by saying she thinks we can make cuts that are “surgical, with a scalpel” rather than “lopping great chunks out.”

We have to lose Lydia and Mrs. Forster sea-bathing, but I’ve insisted we keep the sea-bathing machines. Devastatingly, we’re losing Mr. Collins sneaking out of Longbourn down a drainpipe—a day of shooting for one moment of slapstick. Ongoing debate about whether we can keep Lizzy and Jane finding the Netherfield flushing toilet. There aren’t any original Georgian ones around and it will cost £15k to build. Discussion of whether £15k is too expensive for a joke. I think not, but then I have regularly lost much more, dignity-wise if not financially, to secure a laugh.
